title: Barbourville, the Knox County seat on the Cumberland
summary: Knox County was formed on December 19, 1799, and James Barbour’s gift of 38 acres became its seat, a Wilderness Road town that saw eastern Kentucky’s first Civil War skirmish in 1861.
bodyMarkdown:
Barbourville sits in the valley of the upper Cumberland River, where Richland Creek comes in, near the middle of Knox County. For most of its life the town has risen and stalled with the roads that ran past it.

## A county and a gift of land

The General Assembly [created Knox County on December 19, 1799](https://scholarworks.moreheadstate.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1385&context=kentucky_county_histories), carving it entirely out of Lincoln County. It was Kentucky’s forty-first county, and at first it reached across some 2,300 square miles of the upper Cumberland country. Over the following decades Clay, Rockcastle, Whitley, Harlan, Laurel, and Bell counties took pieces of it in turn, until by 1882 it was down to 388 square miles.

The name is usually credited to [Henry Knox](https://grokipedia.com/page/Henry_Knox), Washington’s artillery chief and first secretary of war, though some twentieth-century historians argued for the long hunter [James Knox](/stories/james-knox/), who sat in the state senate for Lincoln County when the county was formed.

A county needed a seat. James Barbour, a Virginia-born settler, [offered 38 acres of his 5,000-acre holding](https://scholarworks.moreheadstate.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1385&context=kentucky_county_histories) for one, and the town laid out there [in 1800 took his name](https://nkaa.uky.edu/nkaa/items/show/2409). It grew up beside Richard Ballinger’s tavern, a well-known stop on the [Wilderness Road](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wilderness_Road), and its post office opened on April 1, 1804.

In 1800 the whole county counted 1,109 people, 62 of them enslaved. The legislature [formally established the town in 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbourville,_Kentucky).

The ground had a longer story. Half a century earlier, in April 1750, Dr. Thomas Walker’s exploring party had raised a small log cabin a few miles away; the [KHS marker for that first cabin](https://history.ky.gov/markers/first-cabin-in-kentucky) stands in town, and his trip is told in its own [Cumberland Gap story](/stories/thomas-walker-and-cumberland-gap/).

## A small mountain town

Growth came slowly. By about 1840 Barbourville had [some 224 residents](https://grokipedia.com/page/Barbourville,_Kentucky), a handful of stores, a tavern, three churches, a school, and the courthouse. In those years a young doctor named [Samuel Freeman Miller](https://grokipedia.com/page/Samuel_Freeman_Miller) practiced medicine here, read law in a shared office, and took on a few cases before leaving for Iowa; he later sat on the U.S. Supreme Court.

## The fight at the bridge

The Civil War arrived early. Through the summer of 1861, Unionists from Kentucky and East Tennessee drilled at Camp Andrew Johnson near town. On the foggy morning of [September 19, 1861](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Barbourville), about 800 Confederates under Col. Joel A. Battle, sent by Gen. [Felix Zollicoffer](https://grokipedia.com/page/Felix_Zollicoffer), came up from Cumberland Ford. Most of the recruits had already left for Camp Dick Robinson.

About 300 Home Guards under Capt. Isaac J. Black pulled the planks off the bridge and held the crossing until they were driven off. The [KHS marker](https://history.ky.gov/markers/civil-war-actions) calls it the first skirmish in eastern Kentucky, and it is counted as the first Confederate victory in the state. The raiders burned the camp, and a month later the campaign was checked at [Camp Wildcat](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Camp_Wildcat).

## Kentucky today

Union College opened in 1879, the railroad reached town in 1888, and the college carries on as Union Commonwealth University. Markers for the 1861 fight stand in Barbourville’s Civil War park, and the pin sits there.
